questions.stem: Identify the three parts of an argument.
options: The claim, the reason, the conclusion
The mess, the symptom, the problem
The cause, the effect, the fix
The premise, the evidence, the assumption
questions.why: Three words are enough to separate the parts. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Describe the claim.
options: What someone wants you to accept — 'we should close the Deira branch'
The evidence or argument offered in support — 'it has lost money for three quarters'
What follows if the reason holds — 'closing it will improve total profit'
The unstated sentence that must be true for the argument to work
questions.why: Claim = what you are asked to accept. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Describe the reason.
options: The evidence or argument offered for the claim — 'it has lost money for three quarters'
What someone wants you to accept — 'we should close the Deira branch'
The final decision taken at the end of the meeting once the whole argument has been heard by everyone
The hidden sentence that nobody said but that the whole argument depends on
questions.why: Reason = the evidence offered. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Describe the conclusion.
options: What follows if the reason holds — 'closing it will improve total profit'
The evidence offered for the claim — 'the branch has lost money for three quarters'
The first sentence of the proposal, which states what the speaker wants
The budget that would be freed if the claim were accepted
questions.why: Conclusion = what follows if the reason holds. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Explain what happens when someone writes the three lines out in front of a meeting.
options: Half of all bad arguments collapse
The meeting gets longer, because every line has to be agreed
Everyone agrees, because the argument is now clear to all
The claim is proved, because the three parts are in place
questions.why: Writing them separately is the first thing to do with any proposal. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Explain why asking 'what is the reason?' is a complete contribution to a meeting.
options: If no reason can be found, there may not be one
It ends the meeting, because nobody can answer it
It is polite only, and has no effect on the decision
It proves the claim, because a reason is always found
questions.why: Saying it politely is enough. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Identify the four moves for testing any argument, in order.
options: What is claimed? What is assumed? Does the reason support the claim? How good is the evidence?
Who said it? When did they say it? Where did they say it? How much will it cost?
Agree with what is true, disagree with what is false, vote on the rest, then act
What is the claim? What will it cost? What is the benefit? What is the risk?
questions.why: Order matters: move 2 kills more bad arguments than move 4. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Explain why move 2 is run before move 4.
options: Finding the assumption kills more bad arguments than attacking the evidence, and it costs nothing
Evidence is never important, because any evidence can be found to support any claim
Move 4 is the hardest and should be left until the group is warmed up
Move 2 is faster to type into the notes, so it comes first in the record
questions.why: People usually attack the evidence first. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Describe move 1.
options: State the claim in one sentence in your own words and check the speaker agrees
Attack the evidence offered for the claim and ask for its source, size and date
Find the budget that would be needed if the claim were accepted
Vote on whether the claim should be accepted before discussing it
questions.why: Move 1: what exactly is being claimed. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Describe move 3.
options: Check whether the reason actually supports the claim — a true reason can support a different conclusion
Find the assumption that sits between the reason and the claim and ask whether it was checked
Judge the evidence source and ask whether the people who produced it wanted a result
State the claim in your own words and check that the speaker agrees with the wording
questions.why: Move 3: does the reason support the claim. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Explain where the four moves should be used on your own work.
options: On your own project report before the instructor does
Only on others' proposals, because you already know your own reasoning
Never — they are for the exam and not for real work
Only in meetings, where arguments are made out loud
questions.why: Every mark in section 3 depends on them. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Describe an assumption.
options: The sentence that must be true for the reason to support the claim — and which nobody said
The claim itself, restated in the speaker's own words
The evidence offered in support of the claim
The conclusion that follows if the reason holds
questions.why: The invisible sentence. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the unstated assumption in 'staff are unhappy, so raise pay'.
options: Pay is what they are unhappy about
Staff deserve more than they are currently paid
The company can afford to raise pay this year
Unhappy staff leave for better-paid jobs elsewhere
questions.why: The sentence between the reason and the claim. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the unstated assumption in 'competitors have an app, so build an app'.
options: Their app is why they are winning
Apps are expensive to build and maintain
Customers like apps and expect every business to have one
We have developers who could build an app in time
questions.why: Nobody said it, and nobody checked it. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the unstated assumption in 'sales fell after March, so the March change caused it'.
options: Nothing else changed in March
Sales always fall in March because of the season
The change was bad for customers and should be reversed
Customers noticed the change and reacted to it
questions.why: Nothing else changed — has anyone checked? See §4.3.

questions.stem: Describe how to find an assumption.
options: Ask 'what would have to be true for this reason to lead to this claim?' then ask whether anyone checked it
Ask who said it and whether they have the authority to make the claim
Ask how much the claim would cost if it were accepted and acted on
Ask the customer whether the claim matches their experience of the business
questions.why: Then ask whether it has been checked. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the four tests for evidence.
options: Source, size, age, fit
Cost, speed, quality, risk
Who, what, where, when
Claim, reason, assumption, conclusion
questions.why: A vocabulary for saying what is wrong without saying 'I disagree'. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Describe the source test.
options: Who produced it, and did they want a result?
How many observations does it rest on?
Is it still true of this situation today?
Is it evidence for this claim, or for a neighbouring one?
questions.why: A supplier's own study of its product is a weak answer. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Describe the fit test.
options: Is it evidence for THIS claim?
Is it recent enough to still be true?
Is it large enough to be trusted?
Is it from a source with no interest in the result?
questions.why: Satisfaction data used to argue about price fails fit. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Identify the most common evidence failure in student work.
options: Fit — the evidence is real, recent and large, and about something adjacent to the claim
Source — students rely on evidence produced by people who wanted a result
Size — students build arguments on two or three observations
Age — students use evidence that was true years ago but is stale today
questions.why: Fit is the most common failure. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Explain what to state beside evidence in a report.
options: Its source, size and date
Only its conclusion, so that the report stays short
The author's opinion of how strong it is
The budget that the evidence supports
questions.why: Assume the reader will apply the four tests. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Identify the five weak moves.
options: Attacking the person, the false choice, appeal to authority, one vivid case, because we always have
Claim, reason, assumption, evidence and fit
Mess, symptom, problem, tree and size
Confirmation, anchoring, availability, sunk cost and groupthink
questions.why: Naming them lets you object without attacking the person. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Describe the false choice.
options: Offering two options as if there were only two — 'either we cut staff or we close'
Treating status as evidence — 'the regional director thinks so'
Letting one story outweigh the data — 'my cousin had a bad experience'
Answering who said it instead of what was said — 'she always exaggerates'
questions.why: False choice = only two options offered. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Describe the appeal to authority.
options: Treating status as evidence — 'the regional director thinks so'
Offering two options only — 'either we cut staff or we close'
One vivid story — 'my cousin had a terrible experience at that branch last year'
Habit as a reason — 'we have always had a branch in Deira'
questions.why: Status is not evidence. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Describe how to answer any weak move.
options: Agree with what is true in it, then ask for the reason
Attack the speaker, because a weak move shows a weak thinker
Ignore it and move on to the next point in the meeting
Repeat your own claim louder until the room accepts it
questions.why: 'That is a real example — do we know how common it is?' See §4.5.

questions.stem: Describe the 'one vivid case' move.
options: Letting one story outweigh the data — 'my cousin had a bad experience'
Treating habit as a reason — 'we have always done it this way'
Answering who said it instead of what was said — 'she always complains'
Offering two options as if there were only two — 'cut staff or close'
questions.why: One story vs the data. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Describe creative mode.
options: Opens up — asks what else could be true or done, with judgement suspended
Narrows down and tests — asks whether the idea holds and what the evidence is
Runs both modes at once, judging each idea as it is spoken
Is only for creative people, who generate the options for others to test
questions.why: Used in chapter 7 when generating alternatives. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Describe critical mode.
options: Narrows down — asks whether this holds, what the evidence is, what is assumed
Opens up with judgement suspended — asks what else could be true or could be done about it
Is for analytical people only, who test the ideas that others generate
Is used only in exams, where there is no time to generate options
questions.why: Used here and again in chapter 9. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Explain the failure the chapter warns about with the two modes.
options: Running both at once — ideas are judged as spoken, so nothing new survives and nothing is tested properly
Using creative mode at all, because business decisions need evidence rather than ideas
Using critical mode at all, because criticism kills the ideas the business needs
Switching modes during a meeting, because the room loses track of what it is doing
questions.why: Say out loud which mode the room is in. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Identify the practical rule for running the two modes in a meeting.
options: Say which mode the room is in and for how long — 'ten minutes of options, no objections, then we test them'
Always judge immediately, so that weak ideas do not waste the meeting's time
Never test ideas in the meeting, because testing belongs to the analysis afterwards
Let the boss choose the mode, because the boss is responsible for the decision
questions.why: A complete meeting design. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Explain why testing your own reasoning is the hard part.
options: It is neither easy nor enjoyable, and it separates a good report from a confident one
It takes more time than testing other people's arguments
It needs software to record the claim, reason and assumption
Nobody does it, so there are no examples to learn from
questions.why: Testing others' arguments is easy and slightly enjoyable. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Explain what it means if no evidence would change your mind.
options: You are not holding a conclusion; you are holding a preference
You are certain, which is the mark of an expert
You have proof, which is why no evidence could change it
You are an expert whose judgement is better than any evidence the others can produce
questions.why: Ask what evidence would change your mind. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Classify 'the Deira branch has lost money for three quarters' in the closure proposal.
options: The reason
The claim
The conclusion
The assumption
questions.why: Reason = the evidence offered. See §4.1 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Classify 'we should close Deira and move its two best staff to Bur Dubai'.
options: The claim
The reason
The assumption
The evidence
questions.why: Claim = what you are asked to accept. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Classify 'this will lift group profit by roughly the amount Deira is losing'.
options: The conclusion
The claim
The reason
The assumption
questions.why: What follows if the reason holds. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a proposal where no reason can be found. Determine the chapter's reading.
options: There may not be one — ask politely for the reason
The claim must be true, because the speaker is confident
The claim is false, because no reason was given
Vote on it, because the meeting cannot wait for a reason
questions.why: If you cannot find the reason, there may not be one. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Determine the move being used when someone asks 'so you are saying Deira should close because it loses money — is that right?'.
options: Move 1 — stating the claim and checking the speaker agrees
Move 2 — finding the assumption behind the claim
Move 3 — checking whether the reason supports the claim
Move 4 — judging the quality and fit of the evidence
questions.why: State it in your own words and check. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Analyse 'the branch loses money' as a reason for closing it. Determine how it can be true and still not support the claim.
options: Closing may not remove the costs or keep the customers, so the true reason may support a different conclusion
It is false, because the branch's accounts have not been audited
Losses never matter in a chain, because the other branches cover them
Only profit matters, and a loss-making branch should always be closed
questions.why: Move 3: a true reason can support a different conclusion. See §4.2 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Determine the move with the best cost-to-damage ratio.
options: Move 2 — finding the assumption costs nothing and kills most bad arguments
Move 4 — judging the evidence settles the argument once and for all in front of the room
Move 1 — stating the claim stops most bad arguments before they start
Move 3 — checking the reason is the only move that needs no evidence
questions.why: Move 2 costs nothing to run. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Analyse the Deira closure. Identify an unstated assumption.
options: Deira's costs would disappear with it and its customers would not go elsewhere in the chain
Deira has staff who would need to be redeployed or made redundant
The other branches exist and are trading profitably
Profit matters to the owners of the chain
questions.why: Three assumptions at least; this is the chapter's own example. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Analyse 'the other branches are profitable, so the location is the problem'. Determine the assumption.
options: Nothing else differs between Deira and the other branches
Locations never matter to the performance of a retail branch
Profit is random and cannot be explained by location
Staff are the problem at Deira, not the location
questions.why: What would have to be true for this reason to lead to this claim. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Determine how to check the assumption 'pay is what they are unhappy about'.
options: Ask the staff, or look at exit interviews, before raising pay
Raise pay and see whether the unhappiness disappears
Ask the manager, who knows the staff best
Assume it is true, because pay is usually the problem
questions.why: Ask whether anyone has checked it. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Analyse 'our staff are unhappy, so we should raise pay'. Determine the missing sentence.
options: 'Pay is the cause of the unhappiness'
'Staff deserve pay for the work they do'
'We have money to raise pay this year'
'Unhappy staff work less and leave sooner'
questions.why: The missing sentence sits between reason and claim. See §4.3 and the opening questions.

questions.stem: Classify a 2019 customer survey of 41 responses, used in 2026 for a closure decision.
options: Weak on age and size
Strong on all four tests
Weak on fit only
Weak on source only
questions.why: Old and small. See §4.4 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Classify two Deira staff saying the location is poor.
options: Weak on size and source — two people with an interest
Strong evidence from the people who know the branch
Weak on age only, because the staff have been there for years
Weak on fit only, because staff opinions are about the work not the location
questions.why: Three customers said so' is the chapter's weak-size example. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a national report on UAE high-street retail decline, used to justify closing Deira. Determine the test it may fail.
options: Fit — it is about retail nationally, not about this branch's losses
Age — the report is from last year and the market has moved on
Size — the report covers too few shops to be reliable
Source — the report was produced by people who wanted a particular result from it
questions.why: Real, large, recent — and about something adjacent. See §4.4 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Classify the shopping centre's own footfall counts from this year.
options: Reasonable on age and size; check the source's interest
Weak on age — footfall counts go out of date within weeks
Weak on size — one shopping centre is too small a sample
Perfect evidence that needs no further checking
questions.why: Who produced it, and did they want a result? See §4.4.

questions.stem: Select the additional evidence that best tests 'customers would not go to another branch'.
options: Where Deira's loyalty-card customers also shop in the chain
More staff opinions from the Deira branch and the others
Another national report on retail trends in the UAE
A supplier's study of customer loyalty in shopping centres across the Gulf region
questions.why: Evidence that fits THIS claim. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's view of a study from 2011.
options: Age alone does not make it weak — what matters is whether the claim is the kind that goes stale
Always weak, because fifteen years is too long for any business evidence
Always strong, because older studies have been tested by time
Irrelevant, because evidence must be from the current year to count
questions.why: Is it still true of this situation? See §4.4 and the opening questions.

questions.stem: Classify 'Either we close Deira or we accept losses forever'.
options: The false choice
Attacking the person
Appeal to authority
One vivid case
questions.why: Two options offered as if there were only two. See §4.5 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Classify 'The regional director has already decided, so there is no point arguing'.
options: Appeal to authority
The false choice
Because we always have
One vivid case
questions.why: Status treated as evidence. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Classify 'My friend shopped there last month and it was empty'.
options: One vivid case
Appeal to authority
Attacking the person
The false choice
questions.why: One story outweighing the data. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Classify 'We have had a branch in Deira for twenty years'.
options: Because we always have
One vivid case from a friend
Appeal to authority
The false choice
questions.why: Habit as a reason. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Classify 'Noura only says that because she opened it'.
options: Attacking the person
The false choice
One vivid case
Because we always have
questions.why: Answers who said it, not what was said. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Select the polite reply to 'my friend found it empty last month'.
options: 'That is a real example — do we know how common it is?'
'Your friend is wrong, because the footfall data shows the shop is busy'
'Nobody cares about your friend; we are here to look at the data'
'So we should close, because customers are finding it empty'
questions.why: Agree with what is true, ask for the reason. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the five meeting statements. Determine the one with something worth investigating.
options: Khalid's empty shop — a real observation that footfall data could confirm or deny
Maryam's authority — the regional director has seen more branches than anyone in the room
Ahmed's false choice — cutting staff or closing are the only realistic options
Sara's attack on Noura — Noura's record on forecasts is relevant to her claim
questions.why: One statement contains a checkable observation. See Exercise 3 and §4.5.

questions.stem: Classify a meeting where every idea is criticised the moment it is spoken.
options: Running both modes at once — nothing new survives
Good critical mode — weak ideas are removed before they waste time
Good creative mode — the criticism sharpens the ideas as they appear
A pre-mortem — the group is imagining how each idea could fail
questions.why: The failure: both at once. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Select the meeting design that uses both modes well.
options: 'Ten minutes of options with no objections, then we test them'
'Judge each idea as it comes, so that we do not waste time on weak ones'
'No testing today — we will decide which ideas to keep next week'
'Only the boss speaks, so that the meeting stays focused on one view'
questions.why: Say which mode the room is in. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a student who says 'I am an analytical type, not creative'. Determine the chapter's view.
options: Both modes are needed in every problem; the skill is switching, not choosing
The student is right — people are either analytical or creative by nature
Only creative people generate options, so analytical students should test them
Analytical people cannot decide, so the student should work on decisions
questions.why: Two modes, not two kinds of people. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Determine what to do with an assumption in your own report that embarrasses you.
options: Treat it as useful information and state it before the reader finds it
Hide it, because an embarrassing assumption weakens the report
Delete the report and start again from a different claim
Blame the group, because the assumption was agreed by everyone
questions.why: Naming your weakest assumption earns marks. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Select the best person to attack move 2 on your own argument.
options: Someone outside the group, who has no reason to protect your idea
Your closest teammate, who knows the argument best
Yourself only, because nobody else knows the assumptions
The client, who will have to live with the recommendation
questions.why: Give the three lines to an outsider. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Analyse a group that says 'nothing could change our recommendation'. Determine the chapter's reading.
options: They hold a preference, not a conclusion
They have proof, which is why the recommendation is certain
They are confident experts whose judgement is settled
They are finished, because the recommendation cannot be improved
questions.why: Ask what evidence would change your mind. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Determine the effect of stating your own weakest point first.
options: It costs nothing and buys the rest of the argument credibility
It loses marks, because the reader sees the weakness first
It confuses the reader, who expects the strongest point first
It is unprofessional, because consultants should sound certain
questions.why: State it before the reader finds it. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Analyse a colleague who states a conclusion with total confidence and no reason. Determine what the four moves ask first.
options: Move 1 then move 2: what exactly is claimed, and what is assumed — confidence is not a reason
Accept it — confidence shows expertise, and experts are usually right
Vote on it, because the group cannot test a claim with no reason
Attack the evidence, because that is where confident claims are weakest
questions.why: Confidence is not evidence. See §4.2 and the opening questions.

questions.stem: Describe the first step in testing your own reasoning.
options: Write your claim, reason and assumption in three lines
Ask the client to approve the reasoning before it is written
Delete weak evidence so that the argument looks stronger
Add more adjectives so that the claim sounds convincing
questions.why: Three lines; if the assumption embarrasses you, that is useful. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Explain how section 3 of the project report is graded.
options: On naming your own weakest assumption — hiding it and being found out loses marks
On confidence — a report that sounds certain is marked higher
On length — the longer the report, the more thorough the reasoning
On the number of sources cited in support of the claim
questions.why: Naming it earns marks. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Determine the mode a group is in when it lists options with judgement suspended.
options: Creative mode
Critical mode
Both modes at once
Decision mode
questions.why: Opens up, judgement suspended. See §4.6.
